findings.title: Cross-tenant IDOR: VendorAssessment update/delete not scoped to organisation
findings.cvss: CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant read+write of vendor risk assessments
findings.description: TprmService.updateAssessment(id, req) and deleteAssessment(id) load the VendorAssessment with the bare JpaRepository method assessmentRepo.findById(id), with no organisation/tenant check. The Vendor-side methods in the same service (getVendor/updateVendor/deleteVendor) correctly filter on TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), but the assessment methods do not. VendorAssessment carries only a vendor_id column and NO organisation_id (entity has no org field — see lines 16-24), so org ownership can only be enforced by resolving the parent vendor; neither method does this. The @Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0") on the entity does not constrain tenant. The controller endpoints PUT /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id} and DELETE /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id} are guarded by hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE'/'DELETE'), which any TPRM user in any tenant holds, so the permission check does not stop cross-tenant access.
findings.rootCause: Assessment lookups use the unscoped JpaRepository.findById instead of resolving and validating the parent Vendor's organisationId (as getVendor does). VendorAssessment has no organisation_id column, so tenant isolation must be derived via the vendor and was omitted.
findings.impact: A user authenticated in tenant A with TPRM:WRITE/DELETE can enumerate sequential assessment ids and overwrite findings/risk scores/status or soft-delete vendor risk assessments belonging to any other tenant (e.g. another bank). This is cross-tenant data tampering and destruction of regulated third-party risk records.
findings.reproduction: 1. Log in as a TPRM user in tenant A (e.g. riskmanager). 2. Identify an assessment id belonging to tenant B (ids are sequential IDENTITY values). 3. curl -X PUT http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/assessments/{idFromTenantB} -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tenantA token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"assessmentDate":"2026-01-01","riskScore":1,"riskRating":"LOW","status":"REVIEWED","findings":"tampered"}' . The response returns tenant B's mutated assessment. 4. DELETE the same id soft-deletes tenant B's record.
findings.resolution: Resolve the parent vendor and assert org ownership before mutating, exactly as getVendor does. Add an org-scoped finder (e.g. findByIdAndVendor_OrganisationId or join on vendor) or fetch the existing assessment, then call getVendor(existing.getVendorId()) to enforce the tenant guard before applying changes.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

findings.title: Cross-tenant mutation of VendorAssessment via questionnaire workflow (unscoped findById)
findings.cvss: CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant write/corruption of vendor assessment workflow + scores
findings.description: In QuestionnaireService, every assessment-workflow method loads the parent VendorAssessment with the unscoped assessments.findById(assessmentId): assignTemplate (line 214), upsertResponse (line 241), markComplete (line 299) and markReviewed (line 320). Unlike templates/questions/responses (which are loaded with findByIdAndOrganisationId / findByOrganisationId... finders), VendorAssessment is fetched without a tenant guard and VendorAssessment has no organisation_id column to let Hibernate filter it. The corresponding endpoints (POST /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id}/assign-template, /responses, /complete, /review) only require hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE'), held by every TPRM writer in every tenant. A user in tenant A can therefore reference an assessment id owned by tenant B and: flip its workflow_status to IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/REVIEWED, overwrite its templateId/totalQuestions/answeredCount, and (when the foreign assessment has no template, so the template-mismatch guard at line 246 is skipped) write a response row and trigger recomputeAssessment, which saves a recomputed computedScorePct/riskScore/riskRating onto tenant B's assessment.
findings.rootCause: VendorAssessment is loaded by id alone with no derivation of the owning organisation (it has no organisation_id and no parent-vendor org check), so tenant isolation is not enforced on the assessment object even though the questionnaire child entities are correctly org-scoped.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant integrity violation: an attacker in one tenant can corrupt the workflow state and computed risk scores of another tenant's third-party risk assessments, and prematurely mark them COMPLETED/REVIEWED — undermining the integrity of regulated vendor-risk records and audit trails.
findings.reproduction: 1. Authenticate as a TPRM writer in tenant A. 2. Pick an assessment id belonging to tenant B. 3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/assessments/{idFromTenantB}/review -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tenantA token>' . If tenant B's assessment is COMPLETED, its workflow_status flips to REVIEWED under tenant A's action. The /complete and /assign-template endpoints similarly mutate it.
findings.resolution: Resolve the assessment through a tenant-aware path. Either add organisation_id to vendor_assessments and load via findByIdAndOrganisationId, or add a private helper that loads the assessment, then validates the owning vendor's org (vendorRepo.findById(va.getVendorId()).filter org == current). Apply it in assignTemplate, upsertResponse, markComplete, markReviewed and recomputeAssessment.
findings.patchBefore:
VendorAssessment va = assessments.findById(assessmentId)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("VendorAssessment not found: " + assessmentId));
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

findings.title: Missing function-level authorization on third-party cyber-assessment endpoints (isAuthenticated only)
findings.cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — any authenticated user can create/approve/retire vendor cyber assessments within their org
findings.description: Every endpoint on ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController (GET list, GET /{id}, POST create, POST /{id}/posture, POST /{id}/submit, POST /{id}/approve, POST /{id}/retire) is annotated only with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). There is no module/action permission (no hasPermission('TPRM',...) / role guard), unlike the rest of the audited TPRM surface which uses hasPermission('TPRM','READ'/'WRITE') or explicit hasAnyRole(...) lists. As a result any authenticated principal — regardless of whether they have any TPRM entitlement (e.g. an AUDITOR, a read-only user, or a user from an unrelated module) — can read, create, edit, submit, and crucially APPROVE and RETIRE third-party cyber risk assessments. The service is correctly tenant-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so the exposure is confined to the caller's own organisation, but it is a clear privilege/function-level authorization gap (anyone can self-approve risk acceptance).
findings.rootCause: Authorization on this controller was stubbed with isAuthenticated() and never tightened to a module permission or approver role, in contrast to the platform-wide hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') convention.
findings.impact: Within a tenant, the segregation-of-duties intent of an approve step is voided: a low-privileged user can move a third-party cyber assessment to APPROVED (formal risk acceptance) or RETIRED, and can create/alter posture data that feeds the residual-risk tier. This weakens governance over vendor cyber risk decisions and the associated audit trail.
findings.reproduction: 1. Log in as any authenticated user that has NO TPRM permission (e.g. a user with only a non-TPRM role). 2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/tprm/cyber-assessments/{id}/approve -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"approverName":"attacker"}' . The assessment transitions to APPROVED.
findings.resolution: Replace isAuthenticated() with the platform permission convention: hasPermission('TPRM','READ') on reads, hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE') on create/posture/submit, and a tighter approver guard (e.g. hasAnyRole('CISO','RISK_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN') or hasPermission('TPRM','APPROVE')) on approve/retire.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

findings.title: Mass assignment and missing input validation: JPA entities bound directly as request bodies
findings.cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — client-controlled internal fields + unvalidated input
findings.description: The legacy TprmController binds the persistence @Entity types directly as @RequestBody (createVendor(@RequestBody Vendor), updateVendor(@RequestBody Vendor), createAssessment(@RequestBody VendorAssessment), updateAssessment(@RequestBody VendorAssessment)) with no @Valid and no DTO layer. This is inconsistent with the rest of the audited modules (cpty, openbanking, outsourcing, bcp_attestation) which all use validated request DTOs. Two concrete weaknesses follow: (1) Mass assignment — a client can supply id, externalId, isDeleted, createdAt (Vendor) or id, externalId, isDeleted, workflowStatus, computedScorePct (VendorAssessment) in the JSON body; createVendor saves the entity as-is (only organisationId is overwritten server-side). A client could, for example, POST a vendor with isDeleted=true or seed arbitrary externalId/createdAt. (2) No bean validation — vendorName, riskRating, status, emails, etc. are persisted with no @NotBlank/@Size/@Email/enum checks, so malformed or oversized values reach the database and the bilingual/workflow invariants are not enforced at the boundary.
findings.rootCause: No DTO/validation layer for the original vendors/assessments endpoints; the JPA entity doubles as the API contract, exposing internal/managed columns to client binding.
findings.impact: Lower than the IDOR findings because organisationId is forced server-side, but a client can set internal-state fields (e.g. isDeleted, workflowStatus, computedScorePct) and inject unvalidated/oversized data, leading to inconsistent records and bypass of workflow/scoring invariants. Combined with SEC-TPRM-001, the lack of validation widens the tampering surface.
findings.reproduction: 1. As a TPRM writer, POST /api/v1/tprm/vendors with body {"vendorName":"x","isDeleted":true} — the row is created already soft-deleted. 2. POST /api/v1/tprm/assessments with {"vendorId":<own>,"assessmentDate":"2026-01-01","workflowStatus":"REVIEWED","computedScorePct":0} — workflow/score fields are accepted directly, bypassing the questionnaire engine that is supposed to own them.
findings.resolution: Introduce VendorCreate/Update and AssessmentCreate/Update DTOs with Jakarta constraints (@NotBlank, @Size, @Email, allowed-value checks) and @Valid on the controller params; map only whitelisted fields in the service. Never bind JPA entities directly to request bodies.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)

findings.title: Public token-authenticated vendor-portal endpoints lack expiry, rate-limiting, and leak PII
findings.cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — unauthenticated endpoints; bounded by 122-bit unguessable token
findings.description: GET /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/{token} and POST /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/{token}/submit are @PreAuthorize("permitAll()") — fully unauthenticated. The opaque token is the only credential. Mitigating factors: the token is a random UUIDv4 (submissionToken = UUID.randomUUID(), ~122 bits of entropy, not enumerable) and getByToken/submitByToken/doSubmit resolve the row by token and enforce a state guard (guardSubmit allows only INVITED/REMINDED/OVERDUE/REJECTED). Residual weaknesses: (1) the token never expires and is not single-use/rotated after submission, so a leaked URL (referrer logs, email forwarding, browser history, proxy logs) is replayable indefinitely; (2) the permitAll() submit endpoint has no rate-limiting or abuse audit (the controller Javadoc itself defers rate-limit/audit/MFA-bind to a follow-up); (3) the AttestationResponse returned by the public getByToken includes submitted-by contact name/email (PII), evidence file path/name, and the submissionToken itself, so anyone with the token reads vendor contact PII and internal evidence paths.
findings.rootCause: v1 vendor-portal design intentionally treats the bearer token as the sole credential without expiry, single-use semantics, rate-limiting, or response field minimization for the unauthenticated path.
findings.impact: If a submission URL leaks, an outsider can read the vendor's contact PII and evidence file path and (while the row is in a submittable state) overwrite the attested RTO/MTPD/BCP test data. Brute force is impractical due to the 122-bit token, so this is defense-in-depth rather than a directly exploitable break, hence Low.
findings.reproduction: 1. Obtain a submission token (e.g. from a forwarded vendor email or logs). 2. curl http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/<uuid> with no Authorization header — returns the attestation incl. submittedByContactEmail, evidenceFilePath and the token. 3. curl -X POST .../by-token/<uuid>/submit with a JSON body overwrites the attestation while it is INVITED/REMINDED/OVERDUE/REJECTED.
findings.resolution: Add an expiry (token_expires_at) and reject expired tokens; make the token single-use (rotate/invalidate after SUBMITTED); add rate-limiting + audit on the permitAll() submit path; and minimize the by-token response (omit submissionToken and trim contact PII / internal evidence paths for the unauthenticated view).
references: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

findings.title: Unbounded client-controlled page size on list endpoints (resource exhaustion)
findings.cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — authenticated DoS via large page size
findings.description: Several list endpoints accept a client-supplied size request param with a default but no upper bound, passing it straight into PageRequest.of(page, size): ObController.listApiCalls/listTpps/listConsents/listIncidents, CptyController.list, and ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController.list (size default 100, no @Max). A caller can request size=1000000 and force the backend to materialize and serialize an arbitrarily large result set in one query. The TprmController vendor list uses @PageableDefault(size=20) but also has no max-page-size cap configured. These are authenticated endpoints, so impact is limited to authorized users, but a single tenant user can degrade the service for the shared backend.
findings.rootCause: No maximum page-size clamp on raw int size params (and no global spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size), so the client fully controls fetch size.
findings.impact: An authenticated user can issue size=1000000 against api-calls (an append-only high-volume table) and similar endpoints, causing large heap allocation, slow queries, and potential OOM/GC pressure affecting all tenants on the shared instance.
findings.reproduction: curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/openbanking/api-calls?page=0&size=1000000' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' — the server attempts to fetch and serialize up to a million rows.
findings.resolution: Clamp the page size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) in each controller/service, or set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size globally and prefer Pageable params with @PageableDefault plus a configured max.
references: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
